claim.pdf_says: The whole block from 'NOTE   The UTF-16 format of ISO/IEC 10646 is a coded character set ...' through '... consistent with the needs of their application.' is printed in the smaller NOTE typeface and indented to the body margin of numbered item 2). This includes the two dashed sub-items and BOTH trailing paragraphs: 'These techniques facilitate efficient processing of data as fixed-size two-octet code elements, but present opportunities for corruption of data if not handled correctly. To achieve a better understanding, see ISO/IEC 10646.' and 'COBOL does not provide any special handling or recognition of surrogate pairs; nor does COBOL provide recognition of composite sequences. Each two-octet code element of UTF-16 is treated in COBOL as though it were itself a character. Users are responsible for ensuring that any truncation, replacement, or reference-modification that occurs is consistent with the needs of their application.' Font-size measurement at 300 dpi confirms both trailing paragraphs are set in the same reduced NOTE face as the 'NOTE' paragraph and are markedly smaller than item 2)'s own text.
claim.markdown_says: Only the first paragraph carries the NOTE label ('NOTE The UTF-16 format of ISO/IEC 10646 is a coded character set ...'). The two dashed sub-items and then both trailing paragraphs are emitted flush at top level, unindented and unlabelled, so 'These techniques facilitate efficient processing of data ...' and 'COBOL does not provide any special handling or recognition of surrogate pairs; ...' read as ordinary normative body prose of 8.5.1.4, at the same level as the clause's own requirements.
claim.why_it_matters: In ISO documents a NOTE is informative, not normative. Flattening the NOTE's continuation paragraphs into body prose silently promotes them to apparent requirements. The promoted text is directly load-bearing for this compiler's UTF-16/alphanumeric-repertoire decisions ('COBOL does not provide any special handling or recognition of surrogate pairs ... Each two-octet code element of UTF-16 is treated in COBOL as though it were itself a character'), so a reader deriving behaviour from the markdown could cite it as a shall-level rule and could also mis-scope it: in the PDF the entire NOTE hangs off numbered item 2) of 8.5.1.4, not off the clause as a whole.

verdict.reasoning: CONFIRMED, and confirmed by harder evidence than the claim itself offered. I did not rely on eyeballing the 300 dpi render; I read the PDF's own text-layer geometry with PyMuPDF (the glyph mapping is obfuscated, but font name, point size and x-origin are intact). Page 183 measures as follows. Clause body prose -- 'Each coded character ...' (y=115.8-141.1) and all of 8.5.1.5 (y=512.6-613.8) -- is Cambria 10.7 pt at x0=80.0. Numbered items 1) and 2) put their marker at x0=80.0 and their text/continuation at x0=97.5, also 10.7 pt. Every line from y=241.5 through y=463.3 is Cambria 9.73 pt at x0=97.5 (dashed sub-item text at x0=128.3, its em-dash at 97.5). Those lines are, in order and by line count matching the render exactly: the 4-line NOTE paragraph (241.5-276.5), the 3-line first dashed sub-item (299.9-323.2), the 2-line second dashed sub-item (346.6-358.2), the 3-line 'These techniques facilitate ...' paragraph (381.6-404.9, third line just '10646.'), and the 4-line 'COBOL does not provide any special handling ...' paragraph (428.3-463.3). The next line, y=487.1, is Cambria,Bold 11.67 pt at x0=80.0 -- the 8.5.1.5 heading. So both trailing paragraphs are unambiguously inside the reduced NOTE face (9.73 pt) and indented to item 2)'s body margin (97.5), while clause-level prose sits at 10.7 pt / 80.0. The PDF half of the claim is accurate. On the markdown half: `cat -A` on specs/ISO_COBOL.md lines 7985-7993 shows ZERO leading whitespace on all five paragraphs -- the NOTE paragraph, both em-dash sub-items, and both trailing paragraphs are flush at column 0, identical in position to line 7979 ('Each coded character ...') and to 8.5.1.5's prose. I then tried the strongest refutation available: that markdown has no NOTE-block construct, so flush paragraphs are just unavoidable reflow. That refutation FAILS on this transcription's own evidence. 91 NOTE lines in the file are indent-preserved, and the file demonstrably carries multi-paragraph NOTE continuations at the NOTE's own indent -- e.g. line 15440, a NOTE hanging off numbered item 1) of 12.4.5.11.3 indented 3 spaces with BOTH of its continuation paragraphs held at 3 spaces, and line 23205, the same shape. That is structurally the identical case to page 183 (NOTE under a numbered item, plus continuation paragraphs), handled correctly there and lost here. Page 183 is therefore a local deviation from the transcription's established convention, not a format-inherent limitation. I also checked the other standard refutations and none apply: no text is missing (all five paragraphs are present verbatim, including the correctly de-hyphenated 'reference-modification' across the PDF line break), nothing is misquoted in either direction, and this is not page-break furniture, wrapping or hyphenation. What is lost is the informative/normative boundary itself, which in an ISO document is content, not decoration -- 'COBOL does not provide any special handling or recognition of surrogate pairs ... Each two-octet code element of UTF-16 is treated in COBOL as though it were itself a character' now reads as a clause-level statement of the standard rather than as note text.
verdict.corrected_description: Real, with three corrections to how it was described. (1) The claim understates the extent: the NOTE's OWN labelled paragraph is also flush at column 0 in the markdown, so the loss is the entire block's item-level indent (label paragraph + both em-dash sub-items + both trailing paragraphs), not merely the two trailing paragraphs falling out of a correctly-placed NOTE. (2) 'markedly smaller' overstates the type-size delta: measured from the PDF text layer it is Cambria 9.73 pt against 10.7 pt body, about 9% -- a consistent and real reduction (ISO's standard NOTE face, corroborated by the x0=97.5 vs 80.0 indent shift) but not a dramatic one. The indent, not the point size, is the load-bearing signal. (3) 'the entire NOTE hangs off numbered item 2)' over-specifies the scope: the geometry places the NOTE at the numbered-list body level (x0=97.5), immediately after item 2), and its content addresses BOTH items -- the first dashed sub-item explains composite sequences, which is item 1), and the second explains surrogate pairs, which is item 2). It is a note on the list, positioned after its last item, not exclusively a note on item 2). Accurate statement of the defect: in ISO/IEC 1989:2023 page 183 (printed 153), 8.5.1.4, PDF lines y=241.5 through y=463.3 form one NOTE block set in Cambria 9.73 pt at x0=97.5 -- the numbered-item body margin -- comprising the 'NOTE The UTF-16 format ...' paragraph, two em-dash sub-items, the 'These techniques facilitate efficient processing ...' paragraph and the 'COBOL does not provide any special handling or recognition of surrogate pairs ...' paragraph, with the 8.5.1.5 heading (11.67 pt Bold, x0=80.0) next. specs/ISO_COBOL.md lines 7985, 7987, 7989, 7991 and 7993 emit all five flush at column 0, at the same level as the clause's normative 'The following processing limitations shall apply ...' prose, so the last two paragraphs read as clause-level requirements. Repair: indent lines 7985-7993 by 3 spaces, matching the file's existing NOTE-under-a-numbered-item convention at lines 15440 and 23205, which keeps continuation paragraphs at the NOTE's indent. No text needs to be added, removed or reworded.
